changes.before: Remove only the finalLock line, keeping every worker lock and both joins. Is the final read safe?
changes.after: Protect a shared counter so two workers do not change it at the same time.

before: Concurrent conflicting access to a non-atomic object, without the required synchronization, can be a data race and undefined behavior. We do not run an unlocked competing-write example.

The lambda capture [&] borrows the surrounding locals it uses by reference; count and mutex remain alive beyond both joins. Every worker increment here holds the same mutex. lock_guard locks on construction and unlocks on destruction, including when its scope exits. Its lifetime covers the entire ++count operation, not only a separate read.

Both jthreads are destroyed and joined before the final read. Therefore no worker still writes count at that point. The final read’s extra lock is harmless but unnecessary here; removing the worker locks would be a different, unsafe change.
Expected output or behavior: 200. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Protect two related counters with one mutex and explain which invariant needs the shared lock. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: A data race can happen when threads access the same ordinary object without suitable coordination and at least one writes. C++ gives no valid-result guarantee for that situation. The counter needs protection during competing updates.

A mutex is a lock that one thread can hold at a time. Both workers use the same mutex to protect count. The [&] capture borrows the surrounding variables they use, which remain alive until both workers finish.
lock_guard locks its mutex when created and unlocks when destroyed. Here it protects the entire ++count operation. Protecting only a separate read would not protect the whole update.
The program prints 200. Each worker safely performs one hundred increments. Leaving their block joins both workers before the final read.
The extra finalLock is harmless but unnecessary here because both writers have finished. The locks inside the workers are still needed while those workers may run together.

before.question: Remove only the finalLock line, keeping every worker lock and both joins. Is the final read safe?
choices: No: every read requires a lock forever, even after all writers join.
Yes: both workers have finished, and count is 200.
before.explanation: Joining both workers ends the concurrent writes before the final read. The worker increments remain synchronized.

after.question: Remove only finalLock, keeping both worker locks and both joins. Is the final read safe?
choices: No. Every read needs a lock forever, even after all writers finish.
Yes. Both workers have finished, and count is 200.
after.explanation: The worker increments remain protected. Joining both workers finishes their writes before the final read.
